description.narrative: Projektets övergripande mål är att främja fattiga kvinnors ekonomiska egenmakt för att säkerställa kvinnors förmåga att delta i, bidra till och dra nytta av jordbrukets värdekedjor och processer på sätt som bekräftar värdet av deras bidrag, respekterar deras värdighet, och främjar jämlikhet och rättvisa. Projektet ska genomföras i åtta distrikt i de östra, västra, södra och centrala provinserna i Zambia. Projektet syftar specifikt till att: i) öka kvinnors beslutsfattande på hushållsnivå och samhällsnivå för att hantera hinder för kvinnors ekonomiska egenmakt ii) stärka kvinnors tekniska förmåga att driva och äga livskraftiga, produktiva och hållbara jordbruksföretag och iii) stärka kvinnors röst och kollektiva makt på samhällsnivå för att öka tillgången till, kontrollen av och ägandet av produktiva och finansiella tillgångar för kvinnor, genom stärkta kvinnoledda kooperativ, ökade markrättigheter och ekonomisk inkludering. Detta kommer att uppnås genom en kvinnoledd och kvinnocentrerad strategi, med fokus på både män och kvinnor. Projektet kommer att använda sig av studiecirklar och stödja kvinnogrupper och låneföreningar genom kapacitetsutveckling i ekonomisk egenmakt. Projektet börjar med en åtta månaders inledningsfas, under vilken flera studier kommer att genomföras för att utforma och planera projektet i detalj. En detaljerad arbetsplan kommer också att tas fram under inledningsfasen. Studierna inkluderar marknadsanalys, miljökonsekvensanalys, social konsekvensanalys, analys av konfliktkänslighet, samt en köns- och maktanalys. Resultaten från studierna kommer att ligga till grund för den slutliga utformningen av projektets genomförande. We Effect, Sidas avtalspartner, kommer att genomföra projektet i samarbete med Heifer Project International Zambia (HPIZ), Women for Change (WfC), District Women Associations (DWAs) och Zambia Land Alliance (ZLA). Budgeten för den föreslagna insatsen är 75 miljoner SEK. Projektet kommer att pågå i 44 månader, inklusive inledningsfasen på 8 månader.

The overall objective of the project is to advance women’s economic empowerment to ensure the capacity of women to participate in, contribute to and benefit from agricultural value chains and processes in ways that affirm the value of their contributions, respect their dignity, promote equality and equity in eight districts of Eastern, Western, Southern and Central Provinces of Zambia. Specifically, the project seeks to: i) increase women’s agency and decision-making power at household and community levels to address barriers to women’s economic empowerment. ii) Strengthen technical capacity of women to run and own viable, productive, resilient and sustainable agricultural businesses and iii) Strengthen women’s voice and collective power at community level to increase access to, control of and ownership over productive (e.g. physical assets, land) and financial assets among women through women-led cooperatives, land tenure and financial inclusion.
This will be achieved through a women-led and women­ centred approach with focus on both men and women. In general, the project will work through study circles, and support women groups, village savings and loans associations with capacity building of women in economic empowerment. The project will start with an eight months inception phase during which several studies will be carried out . These include market analysis, environment and social impact assessment, conflict sensitivity analysis, and a gender and power analysis. The findings from the studies will form the basis for the final design of the project implementation.
We Effect, the main agreement partner will implement the project in collaboration with Heifer Project International Zambia (HPIZ), Women for Change (WfC), Zambia Land Alliance (ZLA) and eight District Women Associations (DWAs). The budget for the proposed intervention is SEK 75 Million. The project will run for 44 months including the inception period of 8 months.

The overall objective of the intervention is to advance women’s economic empowerment to ensure the capacity of women to participate in, contribute to and benefit from agricultural value chains and processes in ways that affirm the value of their contributions, respect their dignity and promote equality.The project has three specific objectives (SO): SO 1 (personal sphere): To increase women’s agency and decision-making power at household and community level to address barriers to women’s economic empowerment. This specific objective seeks to strengthen women’s capacity, build confidence and self-esteem. SO 2 (relational sphere): To address institutional barriers that limit women’s economic advancement in agricultural value and market chains. This sphere relates to the attitudes and norms of people within women’s lives and the enterprises women may interact with. The objective will work to transform norms, attitudes and values of men, while at the same time support women to develop sustainable and resilient techniques that mitigate the impacts of climate change. SO 3 (social sphere): To strengthen women’s voice and collective power at community level to increase access to, control and ownership of productive (e.g. physical assets, land) and financial assets among women through women-led local organisations, land tenure and financial inclusion. This objective will seek to support the establishment of women-led local organisations, as well as ensuring that women have more access to financial services including insurance and saving groups. Under this objective, the DWAs and women-led local organisations will be trained to lobby and advocate for increased land rights and secure tenure of fertile land.

description.narrative:
The Annual Narrative Report for the 4th year of implementation, covering the period from January 2024 to December 2024, was submitted three weeks late. Significant improvements were noted in both the layout and content of the report under review. Despite inadequacies in the projects monitoring and evaluation systems, efforts were made to report on outcomes, rather than outputs, which had characterized reports in prior years.
Year 4 was an extension year during which WE Effect restructured project implementation. This restructuring was in response to project evaluations and aimed at accelerating the attainment of project outcomes related to economic empowerment for the beneficiaries.
The results achieved during the year are positive. At the overall objective level, which is To advance womens economic empowerment and ensure their capacity to participate in, contribute to, and benefit from agricultural value chains and processes, in ways that affirm the value of their contribution, respect their dignity, and promote equality and equity in Eastern, Western, Southern, and Central Provinces of Zambia, the following results were noted:
Reduction in Gender Stereotypes: Eighty-seven percent (87%) of the targeted 18,904 women and young women reported a reduction in gender stereotypes and discriminatory attitudes and barriers to their economic progression, against a project target of 80%.
Increased Income: Ninety-one percent (91%) of the women reported increased income from agricultural business enterprises, against a target of 85%. This represents a 65% increase from the baseline of 26% recorded at the beginning of the project in 2020.
Increased Participation in Marketing: In the downstream functions of the value chains, overall participation of women increased compared to 2023. For example, in 2024, seventy-four percent (74%) of the women participated in marketing, surpassing the target of fifty percent (50%).
Notable results per specific objectives are as follows:
Specific objective One: To increase womens agency and decision-making power at household and community levels and address barriers to womens economic empowerment
Increased Decision-Making Power: Eighty-six percent (86%) of the 18,904 women reported increased decision-making power at household and group levels, against a target of 65%. This represents a 58% increase from the baseline value of 28%.
Confidence in Managing Money and Businesses: Seventy-seven percent (77%) of the women expressed confidence in managing money and businesses, against a target of 75%. This is a 51% increase from the baseline of 26% recorded at the beginning of the project in 2020.
Specific objective Two: Reduce institutional barriers that limit womens economic advancement in agricultural value and market chains.
Access to Market Contracts: About 43% of female-owned businesses accessed new market contracts over the life of the project, compared to the target of 60%. The underperformance could be attributed to the drought that affected major crops in project areas, which form the bulk of commodities that women trade in, in rural economies.
Access to Informal Financial Services: Women accessing informal financial services such as credit, savings, and insurance to support their businesses increased. A total of 9,020 women from 566 village savings and loans associations (VSLA) groups accessed informal financial services, against a target of 8,100, reflecting a 111% achievement. This milestone can be attributed to the integration of small businesses with the VSLA model, which inspired entrepreneurs in the rural economy to aim higher, while also removing barriers to accessing financial services. The women managed to record a combined savings value of ZMW 6,541,537, equivalent to SEK 2,523,156 in 2024, against a target of SEK 212,752.
Formal Business Registration: The number of women with formally registered businesses, either as individuals or groups, reached 4,533, surpassing the target of 2,500 by 2,033. This overachievement can be attributed to business management training and focused linkages with the Patents and Companies Registration Agency (PACRA). To sustain this registration, the District Women Development Associations (DWDAs) established business registration help desks at their offices, enabling women business owners to access extended business development services and support for long-term growth. Collaborating with traditional leaders in addressing negative gender norms and providing training in confidence building and managing enterprises has contributed to the observed changes.
Specific objective Three: To strengthen womens voices and collective power at the community level as well as increase access to, control of and ownership of productive (e.g., physical assets, land) and financial assets among women through women-led cooperatives, land tenure and financial inclusion.
Access to Formal Financial Services: The percentage of women accessing formal financial services stood at 44%, against the target of 70%. Although the target was not achieved, women accessed formal loans through microfinance institutions (MFIs), agricultural input loans, and some equipment, primarily using their organizations and land certificates as endorsements and proof of residence and land ownership.
Customary Land Ownership Certificates: The number of women with customary land ownership certificates stands at 5,857, achieving 87.4% of the target of 6,700. This progress is attributed to the establishment of 44 Community Land Advocacy Committees across chiefdoms in the areas of operation. These committees successfully influenced local chiefs to accept and recognize developed bylaws that support land certification, thereby strengthening womens land rights protection.
Specific Objective Four: Increased resilience to environmental and climate change by women, men and youth (male, female)
Adoption of Climate-Smart Agriculture Practices: Eighty-four percent (84%) of the total project beneficiaries (18,904 women and young women) who owned farmlands reported adopting at least one climate-smart agriculture practice. Some of the practices adopted include intercropping (88%), mulching (64%), ripping (79%), and crop rotation (95%).
Community-Based Disaster Risk Management Planning: While the DWDAs agreed and were trained in community-based disaster risk management planning, they did not manage to facilitate the development of these plans at the community level because the capacity building was only done in the last quarter of 2024. However, 5,926 (31%) farmers were insured against extreme weather conditions such as drought and floods in 2024.
